KEY MESSAGE 1...Isolated shower possible this afternoon, but 
otherwise mainly dry and warm. Dry Thursday with seasonably cool 
temperatures. 

For the rest of the afternoon, expect dry conditions overall with 
the exception of an isolated shower through the evening. Tonight 
will be dry with mainly clear skies with temperatures falling into 
the 40s. Cooler air advects in from the north overnight while 
surface high pressure shifts eastward into the region. The tightened 
pressure gradient along with steeper lapse rates should support some 
mixing to bring down gusts around 20 kts, perhaps a little stronger 
for the Cape where the gradient is tighter. 

Surface high pressure settles over southern New England on Thursday. 
 As it builds in, the pressure gradient will relax, allowing winds 
to decrease through the morning. Large scale subsidence will 
maintain dry conditions alongside light northerly flow. A cooler 
airmass will be in place characterized by 925mb temperatures +6-
8(approx 10C cooler than Wed). This will bring a seasonably cool day 
with high temperatures in the upper 50s and low 60s.  

KEY MESSAGE 2...Fast-moving system to bring periods of rain Friday,
followed by drier and much colder conditions Saturday.

Forecast trends continue to indicate a rather soggy end to the week. 
The good news is that this is a fairly progressive system, with rain 
clearing out in time for the weekend. High pressure drifts east and 
offshore overnight into early Friday. Meanwhile, to our west, a low 
pressure system develops across the eastern Great Lakes and deepens 
as it travels northeast through the Saint Lawrence Valley. The low 
is expected to deepen by roughly 10 to 15 mb within 24 hours, 
reaching around 995 mb by late Friday evening. Out ahead of the low, 
a warm front brings an initial band of rain to southern New England 
during the early morning hours Friday, beginning during the predawn 
hours and spreading from west to east. There is the potential for a 
lull in activity between late morning and early afternoon. While in 
the warm sector, anticipate mild, muggy, and breezy conditions with 
south-southwesterly winds. A second round of showers, with the 
potential for thunder, is expected late Friday afternoon through the 
evening with the passage of a strong cold front. Drier and cooler 
conditions follow beginning Saturday morning.

In terms of precipitation, PWATs are quite elevated for mid-October, 
with values ranging between 1.5 and 1.8 inches, roughly 2 to 3 
standard deviations above normal. Locally heavy downpours are 
possible, though the flooding threat is minimal considering the 
progressive nature of the system. As mentioned, warm frontal showers 
are expected during the predawn hours Friday. There will be less 
lift during the daytime; however, spotty showers may continue due to 
ongoing WAA. As the surface low tracks closer to Quebec City, a cold 
front brings strong forcing during the late afternoon and evening, 
with a final round of showers and embedded thunderstorms. While we 
do not anticipate widespread severe weather, there is a fair amount 
of bulk shear, ranging from 50 to 80 knots, and MUCAPE values around 
500 J/kg. It could be one of those days where the higher shear 
compensates for the relatively limited instability. This is 
something we will continue to monitor. As for rainfall amounts, 
there is still a bit of spread among the guidance, though consensus 
is leaning toward 0.3 to 0.8 inches. That being said, locally higher 
amounts are possible, with the greatest potential for more than an 
inch of rainfall across northwestern Massachusetts, where DESI 
probabilities are 15 to 25 percent.

As mentioned, it will be breezy on Friday, with a 30 to 40 knot low-
level jet. However, the low-level thermal inversion will play a 
significant role in determining how much of that wind can mix down 
to the surface. Given a neutral inversion, did not want to mix the 
full strength of the low-level jet to the ground. Therefore, gusts 
of 25 to 35 mph on Friday seem the most reasonable. Behind the 
front, strong CAA aloft sends 850 mb temperatures falling from +17C 
on Friday to -5C on Saturday. With steep low-level lapse rates, 
there will be efficient mixing through the lower levels. Gusts 
Saturday afternoon may approach 30 to 40 mph. Mixing may be further 
enhanced over the warmer ocean waters; thus, Gale Watches have been 
issued for all waters from Friday evening through Saturday evening. 
While temperatures will be mild on Friday, the bigger story will be 
the cold on Saturday. As mentioned, temperatures aloft will be in 
free fall. Highs will struggle to reach the upper 40s to lower 50s. 
However, when factoring in the wind, it will likely feel as though 
temperatures are in the upper 30s to middle 40s Saturday afternoon.
